comparison: Perfect agreement on transition analysis claims (C49-C52, C84). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED, with OpenEval noting comprehensive analysis across behavioral contexts and peer reviewers affirming 'lack of stereotyped temporal patterning' as evidence against communication.

Perfect agreement on cross-correlation analysis claims (C53-C57). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes low cross-correlation indices and self-referenced transitions; peer reviewers explicitly note 'lack of temporal patterning' and 'lack of sender-receiver chirp transitions' as main conclusions.

Perfect agreement on behavioral association claims (C58-C62, C86). Both evaluations strongly SUPPORT these findings. OpenEval notes convergent evidence from four analytical methods; peer reviewers specifically highlight 'relationship between chirping and movement' as 'especially strong and suggestive' evidence.

Perfect agreement on beat interference modeling claims (C63-C65). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval describes systematic computational modeling; peer reviewers affirm the approach of 'relating variables to electric field geometry' through modeling.

Perfect agreement on BEM simulation claims (C66-C67). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes sophisticated simulations with realistic geometry; peer reviewers state BEM modeling 'convincingly predicts how the electric image...is enhanced by a chirp.'

Perfect agreement on clutter experiment claims (C79-C82). Both evaluations strongly SUPPORT these findings. OpenEval notes convergent results from complementary approaches; peer reviewers describe evidence of 'increased chirping in more cluttered environments' as 'convincing' and 'especially strong.'

Perfect agreement on dataset methodology claims (C25, C93-C94). Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes large dataset as study strength; peer reviewers praise the 'staggering' amount of data and 'completely novel recordings.'

Strong agreement on spatial analysis claims (C68-C78, with C77 missing from peer). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of spatial patterns and sex differences; peer reviewers treat these as part of 'wealth of interesting observations' supporting active sensing.

Strong agreement on frequency ramp experiment claims (C43-C48, with C48 appearing in peer R3). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes high reproducibility and individual stereotypy; peer reviewers accept findings as supporting active sensing hypothesis.

Strong agreement on main conclusion and factor analysis claims (C6, C26-C27, C33-C35, C83). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes comprehensive factor analysis; peer reviewers explicitly affirm main conclusion with all three reviewers describing evidence as 'strong,' 'compelling,' or backed by 'strength of evidence.'

Agreement on playback experiment claims (C36-C37, C85, with C42 in OpenEval only). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes systematic experiments with appropriate controls; peer reviewers accept playback findings as evidence against communication, though noting this evidence is 'not as strong' as active sensing evidence.

Agreement on chirp classification claims (C28-C29, with C22 in peer only). Both evaluations find methodology SUPPORTED. OpenEval acknowledges arbitrary aspects of categorization scheme; peer reviewers describe clustering as 'state-of-the-art' without challenge.

Agreement on sex difference claims (C30-C32, with C87 in peer only). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes interesting reversal between conditions but acknowledges sex determination limitations; peer reviewers accept findings without challenge as part of comprehensive characterization.

Agreement on temporal playback response claims (C38-C40, with C42 in peer only). Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval treats these as secondary supporting details; peer reviewers accept findings as supporting broader conclusion about non-communication function.

Agreement on background knowledge claims (C7-C24 in OpenEval; C1-C3, C7-C21, C23-C24 in peer). Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED as established knowledge. OpenEval notes appropriate citations; peer reviewers note 'thorough referencing to past work.'

Divergent evaluations on mechanistic speculation claims (C6, C90-C92). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting strong correlational evidence but lacking causal demonstration of improved electrolocation. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, treating proposals positively as testable hypotheses and 'interesting ideas,' acknowledging dual function possibility.

Divergent evaluations on communication hypothesis claims (C1-C5 in OpenEval; C4-C5, C88-C89 in peer). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as established context being challenged. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting the hypothesis is 'fairly' characterized but evidence against it is 'not as strong,' emphasizing study 'calls hypothesis into question' rather than refutes it.

Both address existing communication hypothesis from literature (C87-C89 in OpenEval; C4-C5, C88-C89 in peer). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as accurate representation of prevailing view. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, expressing nuanced view that hypothesis is being challenged but not conclusively refuted.

Partial overlap on factor analysis claims (C33-C34 shared). OpenEval R1 addresses broader factor analysis findings (C26-C27, C33-C35, C83) rated SUPPORTED. Peer R3 addresses factor analysis determinants (C33-C34, C48, C77) also rated SUPPORTED, with specific affirmation of DF and experience as key determinants.

Minimal overlap on frequency ramp claims (C48 shared). OpenEval R3 addresses full frequency ramp experiment (C43-C48) rated SUPPORTED. Peer R3 addresses broader factor analysis including C48 as one determinant, also rated SUPPORTED.
